title: Crates Into the Leftmost Fitting Bin
statement:
A warehouse has a row of n bins, where bins[j] is the capacity of bin j. A line of n crates arrives, where crates[i] is the size of crate i.

Crates are handled one at a time, in order. Each crate goes into the leftmost bin that is still empty and has capacity at least the crate's size. A bin holds one crate at most. If no such bin exists, the crate is left over.

Return the number of crates left over.

examples.why: 4 skips bin 0 (too small) and takes bin 1. 2 takes bin 0. 6 fits nowhere: bin 2 holds only 4.
2 takes the leftmost fitting bin, bin 0, even though bin 1 fits it exactly. Then 5 has no room. The rule is leftmost, not best fit.
Capacity equal to the size is enough.

hints: This is a pure simulation; the rule says exactly which bin each crate takes.
Keep a used flag per bin. For each crate, scan bins from the left for the first unused one that is large enough.
If the scan finds nothing, count the crate as left over. With n ≤ 100, O(n²) is fine.

explain.intuition:
Nothing needs optimising: each crate's bin is fixed by the rule, so just follow it. Keep a used flag for every bin, and for each crate scan from the left for the first bin that is unused and big enough.

The trap is "improving" the rule, for example best fit (smallest bin that fits) or sorting first. Both change which crates are left over. If n grew to 100 000, the scan would be the bottleneck; a segment tree storing the maximum free capacity per range finds the leftmost fitting bin in O(log n), which is the second solution.
steps: Make used, an array of n false values, and set left = 0.
For each crate, scan j from 0: stop at the first bin with !used[j] && bins[j] >= crate and mark it used.
If the scan reaches the end, increase left.
pitfalls: Using best fit or sorting the bins. The second example shows the leftmost rule leaves a crate over where best fit would not.
Using > instead of >=: a bin exactly as big as the crate fits.
Forgetting to mark the bin as used, so several crates pile into the same bin.

complexity.time: O(n²); O(n log n) with a segment tree

solutions.title: Scan for the leftmost free bin
solutions.idea: For each crate, walk the bins from the left and take the first unused one that is large enough.

solutions.title: Segment tree of free capacity
solutions.idea: Each tree node stores the largest free capacity in its range. Descend left whenever the left child can hold the crate, then set that leaf to 0.

followups: There are 100 000 crates and bins. Walk through why the segment tree finds the leftmost fitting bin and not just any fitting bin.
Bins can now hold several crates as long as the total size fits. Which rule from memory allocators does this resemble?
